text:
An approval screen is only part of the evidence.

CERT-In reports an AI-assisted campaign targeting Indian financial entities through their payment interfaces. Its earlier advisory describes stolen credentials enabling direct payment calls that bypass application checks.

To me, that exposes a distinction leaders should examine: recording an approval and enforcing it when money moves are separate responsibilities. A reassuring screen establishes neither the connection between them nor what happens if a transfer takes another route.

I would ask business and IT owners to trace one approved payment through to execution. Match the recipient and amount to the approved record, then identify what the transfer service actually checks before releasing funds.

The useful test is whether that final check requires evidence of the specific approval, rather than merely accepting access credentials. Otherwise, a review could demonstrate that the approval process works while leaving its relationship to the transfer unproven.

I would judge authorization by what constrains the transfer, with the screen as supporting evidence.
